docs.title: Course summary
docs.text:
• This course focuses on the efficient use of modern parallel systems ranging from multi-core processors and many-core accelerators to large-scale distributed memory clusters.

  • The course puts equal emphasis on the theoretical foundations of parallel computing, and on practical aspects of different parallel programming models. It begins with a survey of common parallel architectures and types of parallelism, and then follows with an overview of formal approaches to assessing scalability and efficiency of parallel algorithms and their implementations.

  • In the second part, the course covers the most common and current parallel programming techniques and APIs, including for shared address space, many-core accelerators, and distributed memory clusters. Each component of the course involves solving practical computational and data driven problems, such as basic algorithms like sorting or searching and numerical data analysis problems.

docs.title: Fibonacci Series
docs.text:
Let us assume the following fibonacci series:

\[ 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots \]

This series can be defined mathematically as follows:

\[ fib(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & n \leq 1 \\ fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) & n > 1 \end{cases} \]

This implies that

  1. \(fib(0) = 1\)
  2. \(fib(1) = 1\)
  3. \(fib(2) = fib(1) + fib(0) = 1 + 1 = 2\)
  4. \(fib(3) = fib(2) + fib(1) = 2 + 1 = 3\)
  5. \(fib(4) = fib(3) + fib(2) = 3 + 2 = 5\)
  6. and so on.

Let us implement the fibonacci series using a recursive function:

unsigned long long fib (unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

The purpose of implementing fibonacci series recursively is that the running time is exponential. To see that, run the following program by clicking the button below:

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int);

int main()
{
    cout << "fib(30) = " << fib(30) << endl;
    cout << "fib(40) = " << fib(40) << endl;
    cout << "fib(45) = " << fib(45) << endl;
    cout << "fib(48) = " << fib(48) << endl;

    return 0;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}
Jump to the code @ OnlineDBG

If you run the code, you should observe that fib(30) will be promptly printed out. fib(40) may take half second to be printed. fib(45) will take 5-6 seconds. But fib(48) will take significant amount of time; almost 26 seconds. All these estimations are based on the CPU speed of my PC.

docs.title: The Execution Time
docs.text:
The execution time is the time taken by the system to execute a task. We can compute the execution time using the std::chrono library introduced in C++ 11. Here are the steps to compute the execution time:

  1. Include the header file chrono: 

    #include <chrono>

  2. Set the clock to monotonic clock: 

    using clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

  3. Get the starting time-point before executing the task: 

    clock::time_point start = clock::now();

  4. Get the ending time-point after executing the task: 

    clock::time_point end = clock::now();

  5. Compute the time duration: 

    clock::duration execution_time = end - start;

  6. Print out the duration time in (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, etc): 

    std::cout << "Execution time is "
          << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(execution_time).count() 
          << "ms." << std::endl;

Here is the complete program: 

#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int);

int main()
{
    using clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;
    clock::time_point start = clock::now();

    // we need to know the execution time taken by fib(45)   
    std::cout << "fib(45) = " << fib(45) << std::endl;

    clock::time_point end = clock::now();

    clock::duration execution_time = end - start;
    std::cout << "Execution time is " 
              << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(execution_time).count() 
              << "ms." << std::endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

docs.title: Printing the Fibonacci series
docs.text:
Suppose that our problem is to print the fibonacci series from 0 up to 47. The following for loop will perform the task:

for (int n=0; n<48; n++)
    cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
See the code @ OnlineGBD

According to my PC, the execution time was almost 40 seconds.

docs.title: Parallelize the Fibonacci series
docs.text:
In this lab, we are going to parallelize a serial program using POSIX pthread. To read more about POSIX pthread, visit LLNL High Performance Computing (HPC) or visit https://randu.org/tutorials/threads/.

To create a thread:

  1. You need to put the task in a function.

  2. The API to create a thread is pthread_create(). This function needs 4 arguments:

    1. When a thread is created, the API function returns (as argument) the thread handler (thread identifier). The data type of thread handler is pthread_t.
    2. Thread attributes to apply to the created thread. For the purpose of this course, you pass only NULL, which means the default attributes.
    3. The function/task to be executed by the created thread.
    4. The argument to be passed to the above function.

docs.title: STEP (1): Define your task as a function
docs.text:
We need to modify our serial program by defining a new function to compute the fibonacci series:

void computeFib()
{
    for (int n = 0; n < 48; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
}
Now our goal is create multiple processors (threads) to execute the above function. However, each processor should execute a sub-domain out of the domain\([0, 48)\).

docs.title: STEP (2): Computation decomposition
docs.text:
Let us do computation decompsition according to the lecture (Listen to the lecture before proceeding):

void computeFib(int id)
{
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
}
where

  • N is a constant identifier that represents the value 48.
  • NP is a constant identifier that represents the number of processors.

Now, let us write the whole program serially, i.e., without creating processors (or threads): 

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int);
void computeFib(int);

const int N = 16;   // data size
const int NP = 4;   // number of processors

int main()
{
    computeFib(0);  // this will be the task for P0
    computeFib(1);  // this will be the task for P1
    computeFib(2);  // this will be the task for P2
    computeFib(3);  // this will be the task for P3

    return 0;
}

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

Remarks

  • Remember the above program is still a serial program. But it can easily be converted to parallel program by adding pthread_create().
  • The program will compute the fibonacci series from 0 up to 15
  • Run the program @ OnlineGDB. It should be executed very quickly.

  • We divided the range from 0 up to 15 into 4 jobs:

    1. Job 1: computeFib(0) (should be assigned to processor 0)
    2. Job 2: computeFib(1) (should be assigned to processor 1)
    3. Job 3: computeFib(2) (should be assigned to processor 2)
    4. Job 4: computeFib(3) (should be assigned to processor 3)

  • The argument in computeFib() should be the processor ID.

  • Observe the range of values to be computed for each processor/thread.

  • The details of the ranges is summarized in the following table:

    Processors Ranges P0 0 1 2 3 P1 4 5 6 7 P2 8 9 10 11 P3 12 13 14 15

    Processor P0 will compute the fibonacci of 0, 1, 2 and 3. Processor P1 will compute the fibonacci of 4, 5, 6 and 7, and so on.

docs.title: STEP (3): Create a thread for each job
docs.text:
Now, we need to run the four jobs in parallel using threads. In total, the program needs 4 threads. The main() function is modified as follows:

#include <pthread>
.
.
int main()
{
    pthread_t t0, t1, t2, t3;  // four threads

    // create a thread --> computeFib(0)
    pthread_create(&t0, NULL, computeFib, 0);

    // create a thread --> computeFib(1)
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, computeFib, 1);

    // create a thread --> computeFib(2)
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, computeFib, 2);

    // create a thread --> computeFib(3)
    pthread_create(&t3, NULL, computeFib, 3);

    // now wait for all threads to finish
    pthread_join(t0, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t3, NULL);

    return 0;
}

C++ may emit an error message if you try to compile the above code. This is due to type mismatch. We fixed this issue in the next step.

docs.title: STEP (4): The Parallel Program
docs.text:
Here is the parallel program: 

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

using namespace std;

const int N = 16;   // data size
const int NP = 4;   // number of processors

unsigned long long fib (unsigned int);
void computeFib (int);

int main()
{
    pthread_t t0, t1, t2, t3;

    pthread_create(&t0, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)0);
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)1);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)2);
    pthread_create(&t3, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)3);

    pthread_join(t0, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t3, NULL);

    return 0;
}

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;

    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

Exercise (3)

docs.title: Data Parallism
docs.text:
In the previous lab, we have distributed the computation of Fibonacci series among 4 processors (threads). Each processor will compute \(n/np\) elements where \(n\) is the number of data elements and \(np\) is the number of processors.

Let us examine again our distribution when \(n = 48\) and \(np = 4\).

Processors Ranges P0 from 0 up to 11 P1 from 12 up to 23 P2 from 24 up to 35 P3 from 36 up to 47

Processor P0 will compute the Fibonacci of \(0, 1, 2, \dots, 11\). Processor P1 will compute the Fibonacci of \(12, 13, \dots, 23\), and so on.

Here is the parallel program that has been introduced in Lab (1):

Fib version (1)
#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

using namespace std;

const int N = 48;   // data size
const int NP = 4;   // number of processors

unsigned long long fib (unsigned int);
void computeFib (int);

int main()
{
    pthread_t t0, t1, t2, t3;

    pthread_create(&t0, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)0);
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)1);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)2);
    pthread_create(&t3, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)3);

    pthread_join(t0, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t3, NULL);

    return 0;
}

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;
    int block_length = N / NP; // divide N to NP processors
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int n = start; n < end; n += 1)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;

    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;
    else
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);
}

When I run the above program in my laptop, the running time will be approximately 40s. This is the same running time for the serial version. So, we did not benefit from the parallel hardware!

If you observe the output of the previous program, you will see that P0, P1, and P2 will finish quickly, while P3 is still running. This implies that the distribution is not fair among the processors. Notice that Processor P3 calculates fib(36), fib(37),..., fib(46) and fib(47). We know that the running time of fib() function is exponential and explodes when \(n>40\). Unfortunately, all data items greater than 40 are assigned to a single processor, which is P3.

docs.title: Changing the data distribution
docs.text:
We need to distribute the data such that the data items above 40 are distributed among the processors. One possible solution is illustrated in the following table (Data Partition Table) (where \(n = 16\)):

Processors Assignments P0 0 4 8 12 P1 1 5 9 13 P2 2 6 10 14 P3 3 7 11 15

The data items are distributed in round-robin fashion. P0 gets data item 0, P1 gets data item 1, P2 gets data item 2, P3 gets data item 3, P0 gets data item 4, and so on. This distribution is known as Cyclic Partition.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Let us implement the cyclic distribution. We only need to modify computeFib() function.

void computeFib(int id)
{
    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") started ..." << endl;

    int start = id;
    int end = N - 1;

    for (int n = start; n <= end; n += NP)
        cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << fib(n) << endl;

    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;
}

/*
   Fibonacci Series

   fib(0) = 1
   fib(1) = 1
   fib(2) = 2
   fib(3) = 3
   fib(4) = 5
   .
   .
   fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
*/
#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

const int N = 48;   // data size
const int NP = 4;   // number of processors

unsigned long long fib (unsigned int);
void computeFib (int);

int main()
{
    pthread_t t0, t1, t2, t3;

    pthread_create(&t0, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)0);
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)1);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)2);
    pthread_create(&t3, NULL, (void *(*)(void *))computeFib, (void *)3);

    pthread_join(t0, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t3, NULL);

void computeFib(int id)

    int start = id;
    int end = N;

    cout << "Processor (" << id << ") finished." << endl;

unsigned long long fib(unsigned int n)
{

docs.title: Lab(3): Preserving Dependency
docs.text:
Lab Objectives:

  1. Parallelize a serial program using Pthread Library
  2. Learn how to handle I/O
  3. Learn how to measure the execution time of a parallel code.
  4. Learn how to synchronize between threads using mutexes.

Lab assignment:

  1. Do exercise 1, 2 and 3

docs.title: Problem Description
docs.text: Assume we have a file that contains one million decimal numbers. We need to read these numbers and calculate their sum.

docs.title: The Serial Program
docs.text:
Let us write a SERIAL program to solve the above problem. 

/*
    This program reads N values from a text file. 
    Then, it calculates their sum.
*/
#include <iostream>
#include <fstream>
#include <iomanip>

using namespace std;

constexpr unsigned long N = 1'000'000;    // C++14

int main()
{
    ifstream dataFile;

    dataFile.open("mydata.txt");
    if (dataFile.fail())
    {
        cerr << "Cannot open mydata.txt file" << endl;
        return 1;
    }

    double sum = 0;
    double x;
    for (int i=0; i<N; i++) {
        dataFile >> x;
        sum = sum + x;
    }
    dataFile.close();

    printf("Sum = %.1f", sum);

    return 0;
}

The output is:

Output

Sum = 49965869.8

The above program assumes we know the number of values in the mydata.txt file. If we don't know, then we can update Lines 25-28 as follows:

    unsigned long N = 0;
    while (dataFile >> x) {
        sum = sum + x;
        N = N + 1;
    }

What is the expected sum?

The numbers in the file are generated using RAND()*100 in Excel program and repeated one million times. Click here to download the file [5MB].

We can estimate the sum of those values as follows. Let's consider n independent standard uniform random variables, denoted as \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\), each uniformly distributed on the interval \([0, 100]\). We want to estimate the expected value of their sum, which can be expressed as:

\[ E(X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n) \]

The key property we'll use here is the linearity of expectation. It states that for any random variables \(Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n\), if their expectations exist, then:

\[ E(Y_1 + Y_2 + \ldots + Y_n) = E(Y_1) + E(Y_2) + \ldots + E(Y_n) \]

Applying this to our case, where \(Y_i = X_i\), we have:

\[ E(X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n) = E(X_1) + E(X_2) + \ldots + E(X_n) \]

Since each \(X_i\) is uniformly distributed on \([0, 100]\), their expected value is:

\[ E(X_i) = \frac{100-0}{2}=50 \]

Therefore:

\[ E(X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n) = n \cdot 50 = 50n \]

So, \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \approx 50n\). Hence, you can test the program several times with different values of N. In each run, you can estimate the expected sum.

docs.title: Only the Master Thread Manipulates I/O
docs.text:
If we try to parallelize the for loop (i.e., Lines 25-28) using Thread model, then we are going to violate our recommendation

Only a single process/thread will attempt to access any single file. See slide 29 Unit 3.

To tackle this problem, we let the master thread to load the data from the file into a shared memory. To implement this solution, we need:

  1. to declare a global a pointer that points to the shared memory 
    double *x;

  2. the master thread to create the shared memory using new operator 

    x = new double[N];
if (x == nullptr) {
    cerr << "No sufficient memory to load the file" << endl;
    return 1;
}

    If you prefer C, unfortunately, the C language does not provide new operator. Instead, we use the standard function malloc() as follows: 

    x = (double *) malloc(N * sizeof(double));
if (x == NULL) {
    fprintf(stderr, "No sufficient memory to load the file\n");
    return 1;
}

  3. the master thread to load the values from the file into the shared memory: 

    for (int i=0; i<N; i++)
    dataFile >> x[i];

The updated code can be found at OnlineDBG. Updated Code

Unfortunately, the OnlineDBG has a restriction on the file size (100KB only). The file mydata.txt has been truncated to 17940 values only to match the file size restriction.

The sum of these values is 901746.3 \((\approx 50 \times 17940 = 897,000)\).

docs.title: The Parallel Program
docs.text:
We are going to embarrasingly parallelize the serial program by dividing the work among NP threads/processes. In particular, we are going to parallelize the following code:

    double sum = 0;
    for (int i=0; i<N; i++) 
        sum = sum + x[i];

The data items in the array x will be distributed among the NP threads, as we did in Lab(2). All threads are going to execute a single task, named computeSum(), to emulate SPMD. Then, we manually assign an ID number for each thread, as depicted in the following diagram:

The computeSum() is implemented as follows:

void *computeSum (void *tid)
{
    int id = (int)(uintptr_t)tid;
    int block_length = N / NP;
    int start = id * block_length;
    int end = start + block_length;

    for (int i=start; i<end; i++) {
        sum = sum + x[i];
    }

    return nullptr;
}

void * data type

You may notice that the function computeSum() has the following prototype: 

    void *computeSum (void *);
This is the default prototype of the thread function as mentioned in POSIX standard. It means the thread function takes an object (any object) and returns an object (any object).

Since, we are passing an integer value, we must convert it from int to void * using type casting operator(s). Then, inside the thread function, we reverse the type casting (i.e., from void * to int).

docs.title: Thread Synchronization
docs.text:
The program in Exercise (1) has a serious BUG. All threads are accessing and modifying the shared variable sum. This problem is known as race condition, because the threads or processes are in a "race" to carry out the highlighted operation:

for (int i=start; i<end; i++)
    sum = sum + x[i];

Therefore, Line 69 is a critical section. Now, it's our job as programmers to ensure mutually exclusive access to the critical section by using mutex (or simply lock). To add a mutex:

  1. Declare a mutex variable (globally) as follows: 

    pthread_mutex_t mtx;

  2. Initialize the mutex (should be initialized before forking any thread): 

    pthread_mutex_init(&mtx, nullptr);

  3. Finally, protect the critical section by using the mutex: 

    for (int i=start; i<end; i++) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&mtx);
    sum = sum + x[i];
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&mtx);
}

Exercise (3)

Suppose we toss darts randomly at a square dartboard, whose bullseye is at the origin, and whose sides are two feet in length. Suppose also that there’s a circle inscribed in the square dartboard. The radius of the circle is 1 foot, and its area is \(\pi\) square feet. If the points that are hit by the darts are uniformly distributed (and we always hit the square), then the number of darts that hit inside the circle should approximately satisfy the equation:

\[ \frac{\text{number in circle}}{\text{total number of tosses}} = \frac{\pi}{4}, \]

since the ratio of the area of the circle to the area of the square is \(\pi/4\).

We can use this formula to estimate the value of \(\pi\) with a random number generator:

number_in_circle = 0;
for ( toss = 0; toss < number_of_tosses; toss++) {
    x = random double between −1 and 1;
    y = random double between −1 and 1;
    distance_squared = x∗x + y∗y;
    if ( distance_squared <= 1)
        number_in_circle ++;
}
pi_estimate = 4 ∗ number_in_circle / (( double) number_of_tosses);

This is called a Monte Carlo method, since it uses randomness (the dart tosses).
